parts:
Looking at Brief_three_live_routes written in the last thread, I was particularly interested in the quaternionic thread.  It said in the thread that "The negative. This is where Stage 0 died, and the mechanism recurs. For a real-coefficient `f`, the restriction `f|_{L_I}` is the same complex function for every `I ∈ S`. So the quaternionic zero set is determined by the complex slice data, and every invariant computed from `V(f) ⊂ ℍ` is a function of the complex zeros. The sphere radii are `|Im ρ|`. "No spheres" is "no non-real zeros" written in four dimensions. Prop. 3.1 of `NOTE_existence_loophole` applies: it is a certificate of Hermite type, and the existence of a certificate was never the question." 

Thinking about this, I'm just wondering if being in four dimensions still buys you something. I'm thinking about the residue theorem as a possibly relevant example. Say you take the logarithmic derivative of Xi, and want to check for the zeros with a rectangular contour integral that approaches the real line. In the complex plane you have to make that contour integral shrink in all directions. In higher dimensions you can have it shrink in one dimension and expand in another. Perhaps that could help?

parts:
Your intuition is right about the mechanism and I was able to make it quantitative — but it also produced a sharper negative than the brief predicted, and it closed §3.3 against the recorded prediction. Note is in the project as `claude/NOTE_4d_anisotropic_cycles.md`.

**Split the question in two.** The residue/argument-principle half dies for a reason of principle: for real-coefficient `f`, the zero spheres are codimension 2 in `ℝ⁴`, so Alexander duality gives `H₁(ℍ ∖ V(f)) ≅ ℤ^{#spheres}`, generated by small loops that each live inside a *single* slice — literally classical contours. An anisotropic deformation cannot change a homology class; that's what homological means. So residues in 4D are exactly the classical winding numbers, one per conjugate pair.

The shape can only matter for things that aren't homological invariants — Jensen-type means of `log|f|`. That's where the answer is yes.

**And there the intuition is correct and measurable.** Any `SO(3)`-invariant cycle is a surface of revolution with volume element `4πy² ds`, so the 4D mean of `log|f|` is a *weighted* half-circle mean, weight forced to be `sin²θ · h(θ)`. The round `S³` gives exactly `c₀ = 1, c₂ = −½`:

`M₃(R) = a₀ − a₂/2 = log|c| + d log R + Re(p₂)/(4R²)`

verified three ways. Two consequences. First, **Perotti's formula does not reduce to classical Jensen** — the §3.3 prediction is wrong in the letter (the "first two derivatives" in his abstract *are* the second Fourier mode), but right in substance: the correction is `Re(p₂)`, the second Newton power sum, a classical functional of the slice. Prop. 3.1 confirmed constructively. Second, your degeneration genuinely buys resolution: modes visible with `|c_n| > 10⁻³` go 1 (round `S³`) → 7 (oblate 4:1) → 20 (oblate 50:1). Expanding the sphere directions while shrinking the real one converts anisotropy into power sums, exactly as you guessed. The round sphere is the *least* informative cycle in the family.

**Then it breaks, and it breaks in the one place that matters.** Hermite is an infinite family of *linear* inequalities in the `p_n` (`Σv_iv_j p_{i+j} ≥ 0`), so cycles can in principle reach it — but the forced `sin²θ` vanishing makes the reachable set a strict subcone. Measured, `d=4, R=3`, pair at `1 ± iε`:

| ε | optimal Hermite detector | best *reachable* one |
|---|---|---|
| 0.30 | −1.0858 | −1.0858 |
| 0.20 | −0.2456 | −0.1940 |
| **0.15** | −0.0815 | **+0.0431** |
| 0.01 | −0.00016 | +0.2698 |

No cycle of revolution sees a near-real pair below `ε ≈ 0.16`. The apparatus is exact on gross non-reality and blind at marginality — and `Ξ` is marginal by theorem. That's the §5.3 screen arriving from a fourth direction, this time as a measurement rather than an argument. Whether `ε*(d) → 0` is the open question; my `d`-sweep was unreliable and I recorded it as inconclusive rather than as a result.

Two things worth your attention. **One loose end that could reopen it:** I assumed the generating curve meets the real axis. A closed loop in `y > 0` gives an `S² × S¹` invariant cycle whose weight need not vanish — removing exactly the constraint that produced the negative. That's a couple of hours and it's the only cheap thing left in route 3. **And where your intuition actually has teeth:** cycles that shrink in one direction and are non-compact in another, carrying integers that jump on a *real* codimension-1 locus, are Lefschetz thimbles. Stokes jumps are wall-crossings — the one thing `NOTE_existence_loophole` §2 concedes is permanently unscreened — and they come with integrality attached. The `ζ` address is Berry's saddle-point Riemann–Siegel, which connects to route 5(a). Unverified whether anyone has extracted integer Stokes data there, or whether that geometry is sensitive to zero positions at all; that's the read to do.

Sources: [Perotti, arXiv:1902.06485](https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.06485) · [Berry, Riemann's saddle-point method](https://michaelberryphysics.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2013/06/berry483.pdf) · [Berry–Keating, SIAM Rev. 41 (1999)](https://epubs.siam.org/doi/10.1137/S0036144598347497)

parts:
It closed rather than opened — three things, including my own explanation from last round. `ROUND8_closures.md` is the new state of play; `NOTE_4d_anisotropic_cycles.md` is revised.

**Route 3 is finished, and the obstruction turned out to be one scalar.** The §7 hope was wrong: a toroidal cycle doesn't escape the `sin²θ` constraint, because that was never a property of ball-bounding cycles. Every `SO(3)`-invariant hypersurface is a union of orbit 2-spheres, so `dV₃ = 4πy² ds` universally — `sin²θ` was just `y²/R²`. Worse for the route, a *single* orbit 2-sphere returns `log|F(x+iy)|` exactly, so the invariant 4D data is pointwise equivalent to the classical data on the upper half-plane. No loss, no gain.

**And I had the mechanism wrong.** I told you the `y²` factor suppresses the marginal regime. It doesn't — the `ε²` scaling is universal, the plain unweighted contour has it too (`−0.2775 ε²` vs `−0.0556 ε²`, a constant factor apart). I'd attributed a generic effect to the quaternions, which is exactly the failure mode the project's own §10 warns about. A control caught it.

The real mechanism is sharper. Because the volume element vanishes on the real axis, the weight must have `w(0) = w(π) = 0`, which *pins* its constant term. Free that one scalar artificially:

| ε | optimal Hermite | c₀ pinned (real geometry) | c₀ free |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.10 | −0.022626 | **+0.180322** | −0.022613 |
| 0.01 | −0.000160 | +0.270126 | −0.000118 |

With `c₀` free the reachable cone recovers all of Hermite to four digits. So the entire cost of working in four dimensions is that an invariant cycle cannot put weight on the real axis — which is where RH says the zeros are. **The four-dimensional volume element is blind to the critical line.** That also means this negative is *not* the uniformity-in-`d` wall in a fourth costume, which is what I expected; the `d`-sweep is moot.

**The thimble line died at three independent points.** Berry's abstract is decisive: Riemann's configuration is "*not... several coalescing saddles, but... a saddle close to an infinite string of poles*" — one saddle, so there is no Stokes phenomenon to carry integers, and the saddle sits at `z_s = it/N − 1/(2N)`, fixed by the Γ-factor, not by the zero divisor. No one has applied a Picard–Lefschetz decomposition to that integral at all. And the repair I'd have tried — put the zeros in the exponent, so saddles are the critical points of `log p` and "RH ⟺ maximal Stokes degeneracy" — has the right shape (exactly critical, formally parallel to Kenyon–Okounkov–Sheffield) but **fails at `z²+1`**: real critical point, real value, both zeros non-real. Refuted, not proposed.

**Route 5(a) closed in the same pass.** McSpirit–Rolen is one-way as expected, and the reason is better than "wrong arrow": their programme runs "*given the extra data of an L-function with a functional equation*," they treat Zagier's original examples rather than the Garoufalidis–Zagier matrix objects, and Bettin–Conrey sits at a *degenerate* boundary of their family — their Definition 1.1 needs analytic extension, and the Zagier/Bettin–Conrey specializations "*degenerate to discontinuous functions*." The one hedge: their Stokes constants encode the Fourier coefficients, so all Stokes data formally pins down the Dirichlet coefficients — but that's a coefficient-list identity, the same tautology again.

Two things worth keeping. **Fantini–Rella** ([2404.11550](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.11550)): Stokes constants *are* the Dirichlet coefficients of an L-function — the "physics produces arithmetic" card made concrete rather than analogical, though silent on zeros. And a cheap new screen that separated three of this round's items correctly in advance: **does the structure's natural degeneration coincide with the target locus, or avoid it?** Route 3 avoids it; KOS coincides with it.

That leaves route 5(b) — Nyman–Beurling — as the only live item, and still unstarted. The order from the brief holds: read the Báez-Duarte/Bettin–Conrey literature, run the Davenport–Heilbronn control, then ask whether anything geometric supplies the density statement. Want me to start on that?

Sources: [Berry, saddle-point/Riemann–Siegel](https://michaelberryphysics.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2013/06/berry483.pdf) · [McSpirit–Rolen 2505.00799](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.00799) · [Fantini–Rella 2404.11550](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.11550) · [Gu–Mariño 2104.07437](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.07437) · [Douaud–Kashani-Poor 2604.19731](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.19731)

parts:
Done — `ROUND9_nyman_beurling_and_close.md`. It closes, but not the way the others did: Nyman–Beurling is the only thing in eight rounds that passed every screen, and it dies purely on having nothing to feed it.

**It is exactly marginal, and that's now measured.** Burnol's unconditional bound is `liminf d_N² log N ≥ Σ m_ρ²/|ρ|²`; the Landreau–Richard conjecture is `d_N² ~ (2+γ−log4π)/log N`. Those two constants are the same sum on the critical line, and I checked it: `2+γ−log4π = 0.0461914`, `Σ_ρ 1/|ρ|²` from 250 zeros plus the Riemann–von Mangoldt tail `= 0.0461971`, agreeing to `1.2×10⁻⁴`. **The criterion is conjectured to converge exactly to its own unconditional floor — zero slack anywhere**, and equality would force RH *and* simplicity of the zeros. That's `NOTE_existence_loophole`'s falsification criterion 4 satisfied for the first time, with the constant in closed form, and it passes the round-8 degeneration screen in the Kenyon–Okounkov–Sheffield shape rather than route 3's.

**And then it's exponentially insensitive, which is what kills it.** From Balazard–Saias–Yor, a zero at `½+δ+it` contributes `log|ρ/(1−ρ)| ≈ δ/(¼+t²)`. Against the `C/log N` baseline:

> **`log N ≳ (2+γ−log4π)·t²/δ`**

A zero `δ = 0.01` off the line at height 10 needs `N ~ 10²⁰¹`. Inverted, the best computation in the literature (`N = 20 000`) can only distinguish `δ > 0.0058` at `t = 1`, `δ > 0.118` at `t = 5`, and `δ > 0.469` at `t = 10` — and `δ ≤ ½` always, so it has **no power above height ~10**. The celebrated 0.5% agreement at `N = 20 000` is consistency with the conjectured constant, not evidence for RH.

Two consequences. The criterion admits no use as a detector or control — so the Davenport–Heilbronn check the brief asked for can't be run numerically even in principle (and not structurally either: de Roton's Selberg-class generalisation gives an honest iff, but her axioms require an Euler product, which D–H lacks). And any mechanism supplying the density must supply the limit *exactly, in closed form* — approximate, asymptotic or physical arguments landing within `o(1)` of the floor are worth nothing.

**Supply side: nothing, with three instructive near-misses.** de Branges is the only sufficient condition from a Hilbert-space structure, and Conrey–Li refuted its concrete instance — the positivity conditions "are not satisfied by defining functions of reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces." That's the mirror image of this project's usual failure: a sufficient condition nobody can verify, rather than verifiable conditions with no content. Connes has real geometry but by his own 2026 survey the gap is a convergence statement he concedes "may encounter serious obstacles." Burnol's Lax–Phillips causality is the only genuinely physical structure on the NB theme and is an iff. No RMT, no Hamiltonian, no Hilbert–Pólya link to NB in the refereed literature at all.

One thing changed on round 1's question, though. *What is rigid, integral, or arithmetic?* — for the first time the answer isn't "nothing": the Gram matrix entries are Vasyunin/cotangent sums, functions on `ℚ` with a reciprocity formula generalising the Dedekind sum. But they're built from `ζ`, so it's the delivery/payload split again — repackaged arithmetic in Weil's sense, not transported. Which is condition 6 of the §6 specification, and it's been the binding constraint since round 1.

Two caveats I've flagged in place rather than smoothed over. Identifying the limiting `d_N²` with the Balazard–Saias–Yor functional up to an order-one constant is my own scale comparison, not a theorem — the `t²/δ` scaling is what the conclusion uses and it survives the missing constant. And my "`ζ(s)/s` is outer" phrasing from last round is **not standard**; a targeted search found no source stating it, so I've recorded that as an overstatement.

Worth writing up, maybe: the power analysis in §2 is elementary given BSY and Landreau–Richard, and I couldn't find it stated — but that means assume it's known until a proper search says otherwise. That check hasn't been done.

Sources: [Burnol math/0103058](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0103058) · [Bettin–Conrey–Farmer 1211.5191](https://arxiv.org/abs/1211.5191) · [Landreau–Richard](https://www.emis.de/journals/EM/expmath/volumes/11/11.3/Landreau349_360.pdf) · [Conrey–Li math/9812166](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9812166) · [Connes 2602.04022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.04022) · [Burnol math/0001013](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0001013) · [de Roton CRAS](http://www.numdam.org/articles/10.1016/j.crma.2004.11.023/) · [Bettin–Conrey 1111.0931](https://arxiv.org/abs/1111.0931)

attachment contents (file names are kept in message metadata)
